Q: C promotions confusion: signed/unsigned vs Windows/Linux A:

#define HASH_CONSTANT 2654435769 is a 32-bit value. It is a decimal constant without a suffix (like u).

It is not in the range of 32-bit int or 32-bit long or any narrower type.
It is in the range of 32-bit unsigned, 32-bit unsigned long, 64-bit long long or any integer type wider than 32 bit.

In C89, a constant un-suffixed decimal's type is the first type it fits in: int, long, unsigned long.

Since C99, a constant un-suffixed decimal's type is the first type it fits in: int, long, long long.

A C89 compiler, like the windows one OP may be using, would apply the 32-bit unsigned long type.
hash * HASH_CONSTANT then uses 32-bit unsigned math.

More recent compilers one OP would apply the 64-bit long long type. hash * HASH_CONSTANT then use 64-bit signed math.

By appending a u, 2654435769u is a 32-bit value. It is a decimal constant without a suffix (like u).

In C89, a constant usuffixed decimal's type is the first type it fits in: unsigned, unsigned long.

Since C99, a constant u-suffixed decimal's type is the first type it fits in: unsigned, unsigned long, unsigned long long.

A C89 compiler, like the windows one OP may be using, would apply the 32-bit unsigned or unsigned long type.
hash * HASH_CONSTANT then uses 32-bit unsigned math.

More recent compilers would apply the same.

Both would render the same result (as long as shift < 32).

For more portable code, use unsigned 32-bit math through and do not assume int/unsigned is 32-bit or narrower.

//#define HASH_CONSTANT 2654435769
#define HASH_CONSTANT 2654435769u
uint32_t fibHash_alt(uint32_t hash, uint32_t shift) {
    uint32_t product = hash * HASH_CONSTANT;
    // Multiplication overflow bit are not saved and cannot participate in the shift
    return product >> shift;
}

Further, using a shift informing the hash is weak as those lost overflow bits should participate in the hash code generation.

#define HASH_CONSTANT UINT64_C(2654435769)
// Best if bucket is a large prime
uint32_t fibHash_alt2(uint32_t hash, uint32_t bucket_n) {
    return (uint32_t)((hash * HASH_CONSTANT) % bucket_n);
}

Q: How can I create a 'listogram' in ggplot? A:

Determining the number of bins that show well on the plot depends on the width of the text, and in ggplot2 that is not known when calculating your bins. You can do it in base graphics since the canvas has known dimensions, and we can use strwidth() to aid in finding a compatible number of bins.

I know you tagged ggplot2, but I offer a base graphics demonstrating what you're trying to do.

Up front, I add two spaces " " to calculate the strwidth() so that we guarantee some padding around the strings. That is one method, there are certainly other ways depending on your preferences. Also, I drop the y-axis by 1 (ave(..)-1 and (brks-1)/max(y-1)) so that we start at 1 on all columns and the y-axis labels.

plot(NA, type = "n", xlim = range(example_data$pooled_robustness), ylim = 0:1,
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "Number of Countries", xlab = "Pooled Robustness")
nbins <- floor(diff(range(example_data$pooled_robustness)) / max(strwidth(paste0("  ", example_data$ISO_3))))
bins <- seq(min(example_data$pooled_robustness)-1e-6, max(example_data$pooled_robustness)+1e-6, length.out = nbins + 1)
example_data |>
  transform(bin = findInterval(pooled_robustness, bins)) |>
  transform(y = ave(bin, bin, FUN = seq_along) - 1) |>
  with({
    text(bins[bin], y / max(y), ISO_3)
    brks <- pretty(y, n = 5)
    brks <- brks[brks > 0]
    axis(2, (brks-1) / max(y-1), brks)
  })

With a canvas set to some arbitrary squarish dimensions on my desktop, nbins is 11 and I see this:

If I make that graphics canvas a bit wider and run the code again (it must be recalculated completely), nbins is now 21 and we see below. (Note that the way Stack Exchange shows images, it might look to be the same width when in reality the height is the same and the width is almost doubled.)

There is a challenge with this, though: if we have too many strings for a bin, we'll get overlaps. For instance, if I take that same width and make it shorter,

To address this, we can attempt to find a font size that will not produce vertical overlaps. This is one method, and it tries a little to be clever about it, but there are certainly better ways to handle it. (I'm also adding family below in case you want to switch to "mono", "serif", or some font supported on your system.)

plot(NA, type = "n", xlim = range(example_data$pooled_robustness), ylim = 0:1,
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "Number of Countries", xlab = "Pooled Robustness")
family <- "" # "", "serif", "sans", "mono", ...
yheight_ideal <- 0.7 # somewhat arbitrary, not over 1, little effect on the results
opt <- optimize(
  interval = c(0.3, 1),
  f = function(textcex) {
    nbins <- floor(diff(range(example_data$pooled_robustness)) /
                     max(strwidth(paste0("  ", example_data$ISO_3), cex = textcex, family = family)))
    bins <- seq(min(example_data$pooled_robustness)-1e-6,
                max(example_data$pooled_robustness)+1e-6,
                length.out = nbins + 1)
    maxy <- max(table(findInterval(example_data$pooled_robustness, bins)))
    yheight <- strheight("W", cex = textcex, family = family) * maxy
    if (yheight > yheight_ideal) 999 else yheight_ideal - yheight
  })
opt
# if $opt$objective shows 999, then we failed and will have overlap
stopifnot(opt$objective < 999)
nbins <- floor(
  diff(range(example_data$pooled_robustness)) /
    max(strwidth(paste0("  ", example_data$ISO_3), cex = opt$minimum))
)
bins <- seq(min(example_data$pooled_robustness)-1e-6,
            max(example_data$pooled_robustness)+1e-6,
            length.out = nbins + 1)
example_data |>
  transform(bin = findInterval(pooled_robustness, bins)) |>
  transform(y = ave(bin, bin, FUN = seq_along) - 1) |>
  with({
    text(bins[bin], y / max(y), ISO_3, cex = opt$minimum, family = family)
    brks <- pretty(y)
    brks <- brks[brks > 0]
    axis(2, (brks-1) / max(y-1), brks)
  })

Yielding a more balanced ultra-wide and short listogram:

(This dynamic process might look a little better for the squarish plot as well.)

I used base R for everything, mostly for demonstration. You can easily use dplyr::mutate (and its .by= instead of ave(..)) in place of transform if you prefer, nothing stopping you there. I don't know how to do this in ggplot2.

All of text(), strwidth(), and strheight() support the font= and family= arguments for controlling the font. What you do in one should be done the same in all, as I demonstrated above using family=.

An optional step is to sort the data by robustness, something like

example_data |>
  transform(bin = findInterval(pooled_robustness, bins)) |>
  sort_by(~ pooled_robustness) |> # or dplyr::arrange(pooled_robustness)
  transform(y = ave(bin, bin, FUN = seq_along) - 1) |>
  with({...})

This will move the codes with lower robustness scores to the bottom of each stack. While there's no way here to infer the actual numbers associated with the order, one can infer the relative ranking.

Q: StreamingHttpResponse being buffered when using uvicorn/gunicorn/daphne in Django A: 
Use gunicorn

gunicorn <project_name>.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000


If you have websockets too use hypercorn or uvicorn:
hypercorn <project_name>.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
 uvicorn <project_name>.asgi:application --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

views.py
Use async if u r using hypercorn/daphane/uvicorn

async def sse_random_numbers(request):
    """
    Server-Sent Events endpoint for streaming random numbers for 5 minutes
    Works with both WSGI (gunicorn) and ASGI (hypercorn) servers
    """
    import random
    
    logging.info(f"SSE random numbers request method: {request.method}")
    logging.info(f"SSE random numbers request headers: {dict(request.headers)}")
    
    if request.method == 'OPTIONS':
        response = JsonResponse({})
        response['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = '*'
        response['Access-Control-Allow-Methods'] = 'GET, OPTIONS'
        response['Access-Control-Allow-Headers'] = 'Cache-Control'
        return response
    
    async def event_stream():
        connection_id = id(threading.current_thread())
        sse_connections.append(connection_id)
        logging.info(f"SSE random numbers connection started: {connection_id}")
        
        start_time = time.time()
        duration = 10  # 10 seconds for testing (change to 300 for 5 minutes in production)
        counter = 0
        
        try:
            # Send initial connection message
            initial_msg = f"data: {json.dumps({'message': 'Connected to random number stream', 'timestamp': time.time()})}\n\n"
            logging.info(f"Sending initial connection message")
            yield initial_msg
            
            # Force flush by sending a small chunk first
            yield ""
            
            while True:
                current_time = time.time()
                elapsed = current_time - start_time
                
                # Check if duration has passed
                if elapsed >= duration:
                    # Send final message and close
                    final_msg = f"data: {json.dumps({'message': 'Stream completed after 5 minutes', 'timestamp': current_time})}\n\n"
                    logging.info(f"SSE random numbers connection completed after 5 minutes: {connection_id}, total numbers sent: {counter}")
                    yield final_msg
                    break
                
                # Generate random number between 1 and 1000
                random_number = random.randint(1, 1000)
                counter += 1
                
                # Send random number
                number_data = {
                    'number': random_number,
                    'timestamp': current_time,
                    'elapsed': round(elapsed, 2),
                    'remaining': round(duration - elapsed, 2)
                }
                message = f"data: {json.dumps(number_data)}\n\n"
                
                # Log every number for debugging (can reduce frequency later)
                if counter <= 5 or counter % 10 == 0:
                    logging.info(f"Yielding number {counter}: {random_number} (elapsed: {round(elapsed, 2)}s)")
                
                # Yield the message
                yield message
                
                # For ASGI compatibility, use asyncio.sleep in async context if available
                # Otherwise use time.sleep
                time.sleep(1)
                
        except GeneratorExit:
            # Client disconnected
            logging.info(f"SSE random numbers connection closed by client: {connection_id}, total numbers sent: {counter}")
        except Exception as e:
            logging.error(f"Error in SSE random numbers stream: {e}, total numbers sent: {counter}")
        finally:
            # Remove connection from list
            if connection_id in sse_connections:
                sse_connections.remove(connection_id)
    
    response = StreamingHttpResponse(
        event_stream(),
        content_type='text/event-stream'
    )
    response['Cache-Control'] = 'no-cache'
    response['Connection'] = 'keep-alive'
    response['X-Accel-Buffering'] = 'no'  # Disable nginx buffering
    # Additional headers for ASGI compatibility
    response['Transfer-Encoding'] = 'chunked'
    response['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = '*'
    response['Access-Control-Allow-Headers'] = 'Cache-Control'
    response['Access-Control-Allow-Methods'] = 'GET, OPTIONS'
    
    # Ensure response is not buffered
    response.streaming = True
    
    return response

urls.py

from django.urls import path
from .views import *

urlpatterns = [
    #.....
    path('sse_random_numbers/', sse_random_numbers, name='sse_random_numbers'),
]

Q: How to implement a strict Content Security Policy with nonce using Apache and Angular (20.3) SSR? A:

If I'm not mistaken your Header being set is of the response not the request. If you want to update the request going into the SSR service you may need to do something like:

RequestHeader set X-Debug-Nonce "%{CSP_NONCE}e"

You should be able to then receive the request header from the server side rendering. I used the documentation at the Apache Docs

The RequestHeader Directive

You could probably do either set or setIfEmpty, depends on how the CSP Nonce is generated.
